h1: Lager, ale and the styles big brewers sell
title: Lager, Ale and the Styles Brewers Sell | Craft Beer School
desc: Lager, ale, pilsner, wheat beer, IPA, stout and Indian strong beer, explained for marketing teams who need to describe them accurately.
teaser: If your brief says "crisp, refreshing lager", it helps to know what makes a lager crisp. A style primer for marketers.
standfirst: Marketing teams describe beer every day, often without knowing what separates one style from another in the glass. This guide explains the styles big brewers actually sell, so your copy matches the product.
sections:
A style is a shared description of what a beer should look, smell and taste like. Drinkers who know beer use style names to decide what to buy. Get the name or the description wrong and the knowledgeable ones notice.

Styles also set legal and practical limits. A beer cannot honestly be called hop-forward if its bitterness is barely there. Copy that promises flavour the beer does not have is a short-lived campaign.
Lager and ale: the yeast decides

Every beer is either a lager or an ale. The difference is the yeast.

Lager yeast works cool, typically around 8 to 13 °C. It also works slowly. The beer is then matured cold, near 0 °C, for weeks. The result is clean and smooth, with little fruitiness from the yeast. Lagers dominate world beer sales.

Ale yeast works warmer, usually somewhere between 15 and 24 °C. It also works faster. It produces fruity and sometimes spicy flavours called esters and phenols. Ales tend to taste fuller and more varied.

Colour has nothing to do with it. A lager can be black and an ale can be pale gold. Our guide on beer styles covers the full range.

The yeast choice also shapes the business. Lager ties up tanks for longer because of its cold maturation, so it costs more tank time per hectolitre than most ales. That is one reason craft brewers with few tanks often lean on ales.

Pale lager. The beer most people picture: light gold, clear, fizzy, low bitterness and served cold. Mainstream Indian lagers sit here, often brewed with rice or maize alongside malt for a lighter body.

Pilsner. A pale lager with more hop character, a firmer bitterness and a dry finish. It comes from the Czech city of Plzeň. Calling a sweet, low bitterness lager a pilsner stretches the word.

Helles. A soft, malty pale lager from Munich, gentler on bitterness than pilsner.

Strong lager. In India, strong beer is a market and tax category rather than a classic style: typically above 5 per cent ABV, often noticeably sweet and warming. It sells in large volumes here.

Light lager. A lower calorie, lower strength pale lager with very little bitterness. Its appeal is easy drinking, so copy that promises big flavour will not match the glass.

Wheat beer. Brewed with a large share of wheat. The German hefeweizen is hazy, with banana and clove aromas from its yeast. The Belgian witbier is spiced with coriander and orange peel. Both are popular in Indian brewpubs and work well in heat.

IPA. India pale ale. A hop-forward ale with high bitterness and strong aroma, from citrus and pine to tropical fruit. The name ties back to beer shipped from Britain to India in the nineteenth century. Modern IPAs are a craft staple.

Stout. A dark ale made with roasted grain, tasting of coffee and dark chocolate. Dark colour does not mean high strength.

A few words in beer copy carry more meaning than marketers expect.

  • Crisp suits a clean lager with a dry finish. It does not suit a sweet strong beer.
  • Smooth usually means low bitterness and soft carbonation.
  • Craft implies small, independent production. Use it carefully for beer brewed at scale.
  • Fresh invites a question about shelf life. Hoppy beers lose aroma quickly, especially stored warm.

When in doubt, ask the brewing team. They will usually be pleased someone asked.

Numbers help too. Bitterness is measured in IBU. Mainstream lagers usually sit low, often under 20, while many IPAs run several times higher. Strength is on the label as ABV. If the brief and the lab sheet disagree, the lab sheet wins.

Descriptions improve fast when the writer has tasted the beer next to a reference. A guided session with a pale lager, a pilsner, a wheat beer and a stout teaches more than any style sheet. Keep it opt-in and within company policy, with small pours, spit cups and water. Non-drinkers can still smell and assess every sample. Our guide to how to taste beer explains the method.
faqs: What is the difference between lager and ale?
The yeast. Lager yeast ferments cool and slowly for a clean flavour. Ale yeast ferments warmer and faster, adding fruity and spicy notes.
Is dark beer stronger than pale beer?
Not necessarily. Colour comes from roasted or darker malts, while strength comes from how much sugar was fermented.
Is strong beer a beer style?
Not in the classic sense. In India it is a market and tax category, typically above 5 per cent ABV, usually brewed as a lager.
Why is it called India pale ale?
The name comes from hoppy pale ales shipped from Britain to India in the nineteenth century.
